title: Presentation: Batch Intelligence at Scale: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent LLM Workflows with Built-In Resilience
summary:
Aditya Mulik explains how Walmart Global Tech deployed multi-agent LLM workflows across 4,700 stores for nightly batch inventory forecasting. He discusses tackling production hurdles - schema violations, cross-department data mismatches, and network drops - via MCP grounding and loop agents, while slashing cloud inference costs from $100k+ to $10k per month shifting from PTUs to pay-as-you-go.

By Aditya Mulik

title: Edith Harbaugh: Code Is Cheap. The Last Mile Isn't.
summary:
Automated software delivery is moving faster than the people who used to approve every release. LaunchDarkly co-founder and CEO Edith Harbaugh tells Guy Podjarny why rollback should be autonomous, why one-shot coding agents fail, and why the bottleneck has moved to the last mile.

What we cover:
– How automated software delivery and autonomous rollback take humans out of the 2 a.m. incident
– What makes a good feature flag, and when a homegrown system stops being enough
– Why coding agents need an explicit definition of success before they write a line
– Where release management fits in an AI software factory
– Feature flags for AI agents: switching models and prompts at runtime
– Running a company in the agentic coding era, and why teams should take dumb bets

title: Article: LLM Reliability Layers Under Test: Accuracy, Yield, and the Limits of Verification
summary:
Verification layers sort outputs by trust rather than fixing errors. In a benchmark of six reliability layers, voting and self-correction failed to recover accuracy - they only withheld doubtful records. Production systems gain more reliability by replacing generation with deterministic lookups, tracking yield over raw accuracy, and resolving extraction bottlenecks before stacking checks.

By Pushpdeep Mishra, Wejdan Bagais

title: WorkflowArena: Benchmarking Executable Workflow Orchestration in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems rather than as a standalone model operating within a single context. Recent agent harnesses allow the model to instantiate worker agents and to author the executable workflow that coordinates them, shifting the design of system structure from developers to the model at run time. The quality of this organization therefore constitutes a distinct capability, yet existing benchmarks either measure end-to-end task completion or evaluate coordination under structures specified in advance. We formalize this capability as workflow orchestration and introduce WorkflowArena, a benchmark of 145 long-horizon tasks spanning 8 professional domains, from software engineering and formal mathematics to legal analysis and 3D production. Each task specifies an initial workspace and an integrated deliverable composed of interdependent components, which is assessed by a hidden verifier. Agents determine autonomously whether and how to delegate, and all delegation is recorded, enabling joint evaluation of deliverable quality and the organization of the underlying work. Experiments with nine models show that no single configuration performs best across all domains and that systems exhibit distinct delegation strategies: at high effort, Claude models in Claude Code invoke workflows less frequently but with larger worker groups, whereas GPT models in Codex delegate more frequently in smaller units. When the executing model is held fixed on a challenging subset of tasks, workflows authored by Claude Opus 5.5 substantially improve weaker executors, indicating that workflow organization is itself a measurable determinant of task performance.

title: Can the Confidence and Decisions of System 1 Models Be Trusted? An Explainability and Perturbation Audit of Jev-Style Decision Models
summary: "System 1" decision models (pioneered by TypeSafe AI's Jev) replace autoregressive text generation with a single forward pass returning typed probability distributions over declared schemas (Choice, Score, Noul). While deployed for low-latency routing and automated triage, their statistical calibration and post-hoc explainability remain uncharacterized. We introduce an open, deterministic audit benchmark evaluating System 1 decision models across calibration under label-preserving perturbations, cross-question interference, and post-hoc attribution faithfulness. Evaluating five open-weight models (0.8B to 27B) alongside generative System 2 baselines -- both single-token logprob scoring and structured JSON/CoT decoding -- across NLI (e-SNLI), adversarial syntactic shortcuts (HANS), synthetic clinical triage (N=900), prompt injection defense (Tensor Trust, N=250), and an 86-case logic-gate trigger suite yields five findings: (1) provider confidence is an exact closed-form dispersion transform (1 - H(p)/ln K on sub-10B models; normalized margin on Clef-27B) rather than empirical accuracy; (2) bundling multiple questions in one request induces directional cross-question interference (11.7% to 22.4% binary flips on Tev1-0.8B, vs. 0.1% to 0.2% on Tev1-4B); (3) System 1 models with >= 4B parameters are faster and better calibrated under syntactic shifts (ECE_w = 0.030 to 0.087) than logprob (0.144) and JSON (0.378) baselines; (4) for prompt-injection defense (N=250), >= 4B models achieve 0.988 to 0.998 AUROC with up to 95.2% recall and 0.0% false alarms at 48 to 60 ms; and (5) single-pass inference makes 512-coalition XAI interactive (1.3 to 3.2 s/input), while KernelSHAP with a logit link (S1-SHAP) mitigates softmax saturation on disjunctive OR gates (89.3% to 100.0% gate recovery vs. 57.1% to 82.1% in prob space; p_adj = 0.004).

title: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
summary:
Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember

Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as:

[...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.

For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40.

The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others:

Model Prompt size Input ($/M) Cached input Output
GPT-6 Luna ≤272k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50
>272k $0.20 $0.02 $0.75
Muse Ember 1.0 ≤200k $0.10 $0.004 $0.50
>200k $0.30 $0.012 $1.50
Claude Haiku 5.5 ≤100k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50
>100k $0.50 $0.05 $2.50

But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem.

For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis.

And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models:

The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement:

It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task.

(That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!)

Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles. The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response.

Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too:

The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder, which is 40x the price of Muse Ember.

title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
summary:
Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping. The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator, a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room.

Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while:

You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra.

The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.

Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep!

I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound.

Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such.

Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map.

The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.

How it works

When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices, a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract:

We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting.

That sounded exactly like what we needed to build!

Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server.

When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep.

How I built it

I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here's that shared starter session, which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository:

Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve

There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it

I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from

There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app

Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though?

That got me this problem.md file. As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file.

The research looked good, so I told it:

Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else

That got me to this point - most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet.

I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released, and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces.

I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran.

This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients.

On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn.

From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran:

I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate

This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map.

what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...]

Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps

That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps.

each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp

That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound.

The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays

Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for.

There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for

Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is

At this point I was getting close - I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn't it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location?

I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app.

And since I had one spare device, I then said:

add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far

Giving Claude Code ears

I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it's possible to give Claude Code ears.

Claude doesn't have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone.

I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket.

Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem.

I'm reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not.

Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun.

title: Double Blind Evals: Resolving the Dual Confidentiality Dilemma in AI Safety Auditing
summary: AI safety evaluations often involve sensitive prompts and proprietary models. Evaluators want to keep their evaluation prompts secret from model owners to prevent purposeful or incidental data leakage, ensuring longer usefulness of their benchmark. Model owners in turn wish to keep their proprietary model weights and inference code within their own secure infrastructure to protect their IP. We present a way forward for "double-blind evals", which provide cryptographic guarantees that an evaluator's prompts are not shared with the model owner, while simultaneously maintaining the confidentiality of the model weights and inference code. To accomplish this, we use secure enclaves that encrypt data in RAM at the hardware level. In a world-first pilot, we test this approach by evaluating a proprietary Google DeepMind model (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite) against a selection of the private AILuminate benchmark corpus, using an NVIDIA H100 secure enclave on Google Cloud Platform, and using OpenMined's PySyft to maintain data and model privacy. We believe this effort marks the first use of this technology to provide mutual secrecy for one organization's frontier-class proprietary model weights and another organization's closed benchmark.

title: dNaViT: Discrete Codes are General-Purpose Visual Representations
summary: Discrete autoregressive modeling, notably through next-token prediction, has become a cornerstone of modern language models. Extending this paradigm to vision allows visual and language models to converge on a unified framework, thereby fostering shared methodology and infrastructure. This work investigates a central question: how far can a finite discrete vocabulary go in representing the richness of the visual world? We present dNaViT, a Discrete Native-resolution Vision Transformer that produces discrete visual primitives analogous to language tokens. Built upon a frozen pretrained encoder, dNaViT applies lightweight residual modulation with a dual-branch objective to inject reconstruction-aware cues into semantic features. By leveraging grouped product quantization, it scales discrete capacity without inflating spatial sequence lengths, while a balanced training recipe maintains both semantic and pixel-level information. Consequently, dNaViT functions as a versatile discrete visual tokenizer, enabling unified encoding across downstream tasks alongside high-fidelity image decoding. Extensive evaluations show that dNaViT matches or exceeds task-specific baselines across 12 visual understanding benchmarks, 4 generation benchmarks, and an image editing benchmark. These findings demonstrate that a compact discrete vocabulary can serve as a universal visual currency and unlock the full potential of fully unified, native multimodal methodology.

title: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together
story_key: story|title:your experts have partners there s hope for keeping them together
content_excerpt: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used. Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization . Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove. Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance . Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates. Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method. In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers . Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. title: Why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
summary: Explore 3 principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows and how human-review is a strategic imperative for production-ready agents.
story_key: story|title:why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
content_excerpt: As agents take on longer, more complex tasks, evaluating their performance means looking beyond the final AI-generated answer. Human review plays an important role in agent development: it helps teams define what good looks like, evaluate performance in context, and turn expert judgment into data that drives improvement. In this blog, we explore three principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows: defining quality through expert judgment, evaluating agents in context, and turning human feedback into reusable evaluation data that drives continuous improvement. An agent trace is a record of everything an agent did in a single attempt: user messages, model responses, tool calls, and intermediate steps. Teams use traces to debug behavior, score quality, and decide what to fix. Often an engineer or an online evaluator flags a trace when something looks off. The flag is a signal, not an explanation. It usually is not enough to know how to change the agent. The flagged trace goes into an annotation queue . A human reviewer opens the interaction and leaves feedback: did the agent do the right thing, and why or why not? Automation chooses what to review. The human supplies the judgment that builders act on. In LangSmith , a queue item can be one run (a single step or span) or a thread (the full multi-turn session). With a thread, the reviewer sees the conversation the user had, instead of one step cut out of it. Each reviewer brings domain judgment the trace does not contain on its own: what “good” means in that job, what the user was trying to do, and what the agent should have done instead. This expert judgment is often highly specific to the company, role, or individual's expertise, and is a key part of building differentiated agents. Or as Snoop Dogg put in his commencement speech at CSU Long Beach : “Nobody can do you, like you do.” When a domain expert reviews a trace, one of the most valuable parts of the review is their reason. An expert can say why an output was right or wrong, and how a high-quality agent should behave. While reviewers can catch what automated evals miss, they also surface problems that sit beside the agent’s answer. For example, they might discover that an eval is scoring the wrong behavior, or that there is a gap in the rubric. One note in a queue can reveal a broader pattern worth fixing in the evaluator itself. This expert feedback changes the evaluations, and ultimately how the agent is built. title: claude-code v2.1.319
summary:
What's changed

  • Changed auto mode with telemetry or feature flags off, including behind LLM gateways: calls the server can't check are asked about or denied, with no fallback to the built-in classifier; set CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=0 to keep using it (Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry are unchanged)
  • Changed auto mode behind an LLM gateway: CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=1 turns on the server-side check even with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS set; if managed settings set the latter, they must set the 1 too
  • Added support for MCP tasks in the terminal: when an MCP server runs a tool call as a task, Claude Code moves it to the background right away and tells Claude the result when it finishes
  • Added the CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_MCP_TASK_BACKGROUND environment variable to make Claude Code wait for an MCP task inside its tool call instead of moving it to the background right away
  • Added permissions.denyInsteadOfPrompting setting: a tool call that would wait on a permission prompt is denied and the turn continues, in terminal sessions, subagents and teammates
  • Added /claude-api latency-optimize to find where your Claude API code makes people wait and try faster settings against your eval
  • Added the CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FEATURE_FLAGS environment variable, which stops feature-flag fetching without turning off telemetry; every flag then uses its built-in default
  • Added spend for today, this week and this month to /usage for developers behind a Claude apps gateway who have no spend limit, when the gateway runs this version or later
  • Added admin.pooled_conflict_rule and admin.pooled_priority_order to the Claude apps gateway, to set which pooled group budget pays first for a developer in several groups
  • Added an optional login_notice setting to the Claude apps gateway that shows an operator-defined message on the gateway's browser verification page and on Claude Code's sign-in screen
  • Added CLAUDE_GATEWAY_LOG_FORMAT=json to the Claude apps gateway: operational log lines become JSON with severity, time and message, for log collectors that read the level from a field
  • Added a Claude apps gateway boot warning for a case where another policy's availableModels also allows a custom model id that one policy lists by name
  • Added start-up warnings to the Claude apps gateway for policies with no desktopHome that rely on coworkTabEnabled: false or chatSessionRetentionDays, ahead of Claude Desktop's November 10 change
  • Added a warning when your claude.ai login ends and Claude Code continues on the sign-in from ant auth login, which bills usage to your Claude Console organization
  • Added a line at startup naming the Claude Console organization that is billed in a case where Claude Code uses the sign-in from ant auth login
  • Added an "Earlier in this session" row to /tasks that lists finished subagents, so you can reopen one and message it even after it leaves the list or you restart
  • Added a note to /loop confirmations in cloud sessions that a timer stops with its container, with an offer of a loop that survives
  • Fixed MCP servers on the older handshake failing to connect, or returning empty results, because Claude Code declared an extension that it only uses with newer servers
  • Fixed a long-running MCP tool call on a claude.ai connector sometimes never reporting its result after --resume
  • Fixed a session's diff failing to load on claude.ai and the mobile apps when the folder Claude Code runs in has a file or folder named HEAD
  • Fixed /diff showing "Diff unavailable" when a git repository has a file or folder named HEAD at its top level

  • Fixed a case where auto mode was wrongly refused when a client sent a model change and a request for auto mode back to back
  • Fixed /status showing "Auto mode server: Enabled" when the server-side review isn't reaching the session, for example behind an LLM gateway that drops it

  • Fixed a case where Bash deny and ask rules missed commands written with quoted words

  • Fixed a case where text was dropped from informational messages sent to SDK clients

  • Fixed background tasks that keep running after /clear disappearing from the task list in Claude Code on the web until another task started or ended

  • Fixed a case where certificate errors behind a TLS-inspecting proxy persisted when CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC was set. With it set, Claude Code now makes a TLS handshake with the configured API host after a certificate failure, through your http:// proxy if one is set; it sends no API request
  • Fixed claude remote-control exiting silently with status 0 when a first-run question gets no answer (scripts, services, batch jobs, Ctrl+C); it now says why and exits 1
  • Fixed claude remote-control ignoring a piped y that has no newline after it at the first-run question; it now counts as a yes
  • Fixed /rename reporting plain success when the new name could not be saved to the session transcript; it now warns that the new name may not last
  • Fixed ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} not being substituted in a plugin-provided subagentStatusLine command, which can now reference the plugin's own scripts
  • Fixed claude plugin update and /plugin "Update now" not installing dependencies added by the new plugin version
  • Fixed subagents being told after compaction to expect a completion notice for background agents they neither started nor took over
  • Fixed a case where a background agent's later report was lost silently: the notification now says it was refused and how to ask for it
  • Improved config saves on Windows: Claude Code waits longer for a file another program has open, so a kill during a save is less likely to leave ~/.claude.json empty
  • Improved Claude in Chrome after a brief disconnect: it waits up to 6 seconds for the session's own browser to return before picking another
  • Improved Claude in Chrome: javascript_tool results of up to 60,000 characters now stay in the conversation instead of being saved to a file
  • Improved claude purge and the clean-up of old sessions to retry a folder that could not be fully deleted, and to report it as an error if it remains
  • Improved the refusal for a path outside the working directories on macOS and Windows: when only its letter case differs from a path inside them, the message names that spelling
  • Improved the contrast of faint gray secondary text, such as hints, details in /stats, /model and /sandbox, and rejected-action messages
  • Improved the artifact database error when an update targets a document that does not exist, and when the service pauses repeated refused writes
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's warnings about a failed upstream call: each now names the upstream, not only its provider
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's spend limit error: it reads "spend limit reached · resets Dec 1", then admin.blocked_message if one is set
  • Improved the /model picker: older models are now grouped under a "More models" row instead of being listed after the current ones
  • Improved /context at the terminal so the table Claude reads stays short: each list keeps its 10 largest rows, and MCP tools that load on demand share one row per server until they're called
  • Improved /usage in cloud sessions: it now links to Settings → Usage on claude.ai in a case where plan limits can't be shown
  • [VSCode] Improved the confirmation for removing a plugin marketplace: it now checks which of its plugins are installed at that moment
  • Changed MCP tasks to work in the terminal without feature-flag fetching (Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, LLM gateways, DISABLE_TELEMETRY); set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_MCP_TASKS=1 to turn them off
  • Changed auto mode so that a project's settings files or a plugin can no longer switch its server-side check back on once you have switched it off outside the project
  • Changed Monitor's WebSocket watch to follow a rule on every Bash command: a deny refuses it, and under an ask rule an allow on Monitor, bypass mode or auto mode no longer skips the prompt
  • Changed CLAUDE_CODE_PROXY_RESOLVES_HOSTS so that settings files can no longer set it where the host manages the network; set it in the process environment
  • Changed a session's exact Bash or PowerShell ask rule to be refused, not asked about, when a broader deny rule covers the command
  • Changed the Bash tool to ask for permission before running which with flags outside a lookup/display set
  • Changed --add-dir directories to register plugin marketplaces only once that directory's own trust dialog has been accepted
  • Changed nested skill loading: with the Bash sandbox on, skills in .claude/skills folders below the starting folder load only if you start Claude Code there or /cd there
  • Changed self-paced /loop to end when a turn finishes without rescheduling, instead of scheduling a fallback wakeup; set CLAUDE_CODE_LOOP_KEEPALIVE=1 to keep the old behavior
  • Changed PostToolUse hooks to run, with up to 10 seconds to finish, on tool calls that finish after a new message interrupts the turn
  • Changed what Claude is told after safeguards stop a subagent: retry with a narrower prompt or tell you, instead of doing the work itself
  • Changed cloud sessions to drop session-scoped allow rules at a move to a new worker when their deny and ask rules can't all be kept, so you may be asked again
  • Changed the automatic certificate repair behind a TLS-inspecting proxy: it no longer runs when ALL_PROXY is the only proxy variable set. Set HTTPS_PROXY to the proxy's http:// URL instead
  • Changed artifact database saves of rows others may have written: each file gets a hidden marker file, and existing files without one, earlier versions' exports among them, are left alone and reported
  • Updated /claude-api managed-agents-onboard templates to match the Claude Console: removed Performance tuner, renamed two, and turned off web search and fetch in five whose prompts don't use them
  • Removed shortcuts_list and shortcuts_execute, which listed and started shortcuts saved in the extension, from Claude Code's built-in Claude in Chrome tools
  • Gateway: Added startup warnings for upstreams that mix AWS GovCloud with other upstreams, and for base URL variables in the gateway's environment
  • Gateway: Added a start-up log warning when managed settings name an Amazon Bedrock guardrail in a header, which the gateway doesn't forward, and no bedrock upstream sets a guardrail
  • Gateway: Fixed Claude Desktop offering a web search tool that always failed when every upstream is Amazon Bedrock
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a runner started with --use-anthropic-git-proxy or --configure-git registering before a failed startup check made it exit; it now exits first
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed CLAUDE_RUNNER_CHECKOUT_PATH so that each repository in a session gets its own folder: a folder name already taken in the session gets -2, -3, … at the end
  • Self-hosted runner: Removed the end-of-session upload of a session's debug log; a failed session's log stays on the runner host unless --remove-session-state is set
  • [VSCode] Fixed prompts over 50,000 characters being cut off silently: the prompt now stays in the chat box with a notice, and a paste over the limit is refused with a notice
  • [VSCode] Fixed a click on the survey or "Report a problem" buttons sending the unfinished prompt
  • [VSCode] Fixed cloud sessions opened from the extension's Web tab bringing back turns that /clear, or Retry or Edit of a typed prompt, had removed
  • [VSCode] Fixed a deleted session's file coming back when that session was renamed in the extension
  • [VSCode] Fixed Claude carrying out an unapproved plan after a window reload: a step interrupted in plan mode now stops with a notice when the session comes back in another permission mode
  • [VSCode] Improved the "not signed in" message behind a Claude apps gateway: it now looks like an error and has a Sign in link
  • [VSCode] Changed links in Claude's replies that point at Claude sign-in, connector or API addresses to show as text with the address, instead of opening in the browser
  • [VSCode] Fixed a possible chat panel freeze when a dropped item's path contains a very long run of "/" characters
  • [VSCode] Fixed the claude-vscode.toggleDictation command starting dictation in every open Claude view at once; it now acts only in the view you are using, and a second press stops it
  • [VSCode] Fixed the chat panel slowing down while a reply with many unclosed $$ math fences, each shorter than the last, streams in
  • [VSCode] Improved the chat panel's diagnostics tool for large workspaces: it leaves out files with no problems, returns compact JSON, and accepts an optional minimum severity
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed scheduled tasks silently dropping a connector named memory: runs now keep it, mounted under that name plus a short suffix
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed Send now on a waiting message in cloud sessions ending running background agents; they now keep running
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the stalled-setup warning on self-hosted environments: its link now prefers your organization's default or an environment with a live runner, and names it
  • [Code Review] Changed unlinking a GitHub organization to also turn off its All repositories setting in Code Review; it stays off after you relink until you turn it back on
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag setup blocking launch when the channel list couldn't fully load; admins can now launch without picking a channel
  • [Claude Tag] Added a Claude Tag row to the Models admin page for Enterprise orgs with Claude Tag connected, linking to where its model defaults are managed
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed saving auto mode allow rules in Claude Tag admin settings overwriting another admin's changes; the save is now refused with a message
